source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on Kelly Services career advice, Hays, the Center for Creative Leadership and MIT Career Advising.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Kelly Services, Career advancement checklist, https://www.mykelly.com/career-advice/career-development/career-advancement-checklist; Hays, How to ask for a pay rise, https://www.hays.com.au/career-advice/career-development/how-to-ask-for-a-pay-rise; Center for Creative Leadership, SBI feedback model, https://www.ccl.org/articles/leading-effectively-articles/closing-the-gap-between-intent-vs-impact-sbii/; Google re:Work Project Oxygen, reported by Nextgov, https://www.nextgov.com/digital-government/2018/02/google-expanding-its-list-what-it-takes-be-great-manager/146314/; Harvard Program on Negotiation, Salary negotiations, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/salary-negotiations/

cards.title: Start by doing your current job really well
cards.body:
The surest base for any career is a reputation for excellent work. Before chasing the next title, make sure you are known as someone who does the current job properly, on time and with care.

Excellent does not mean perfect or working all hours. It means understanding what really matters in your role, doing those things to a high standard and checking your own work before others have to. Small habits count: replying promptly, keeping promises, being ready for meetings.

This reputation travels. When managers discuss who to give a bigger task or a promotion, the first question is usually "Can we rely on them?" Make the answer an easy yes.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself which two tasks matter most in your role. Do one of them today to a standard you would be proud to show anyone.

quiz.question: What question do managers often ask first when choosing someone for a bigger role?
quiz.explanation: Reliability built by consistently good work is the base that other opportunities are built on.

cards.title: Own the outcome, not just the task
cards.body:
There is a big difference between "I did what I was told" and "I made sure it worked". People who grow fast take ownership of results. If they spot a problem, they raise it or fix it instead of waiting for someone else.

Ownership also means owning mistakes. When something goes wrong, say so early, explain what happened, and come with a plan to put it right. This builds far more trust than hiding errors or blaming others.

For example, if you send out a report and notice a wrong figure, tell your manager straight away, send the correction and suggest a check to stop it happening again. That is the behaviour of someone ready for more responsibility.
cards.apply_it: Think of one small problem at work or school that everyone ignores. Take one step today to raise or solve it.

quiz.question: What is the best response when you make a mistake at work?
options: Admit it early and come with a plan to fix it
Wait until your review to mention it
quiz.explanation: Owning mistakes quickly with a solution shows maturity and builds trust.

cards.title: Keep learning so your skills don't go stale
cards.body:
Jobs change quickly, and the skills that got you hired will not carry you for ever. Make learning a steady habit rather than something you do only when you are worried.

Look at the people one or two steps ahead of you and the job adverts for roles you want. Which skills keep appearing? These might be technical, like data or a software tool, or human, like presenting, writing or managing people.

Then pick one skill at a time. Use free online courses, books, training your employer offers, volunteering, or side projects where you can practise. Twenty minutes a day adds up to more than a hundred hours a year, which is enough to become genuinely useful at something new.
cards.apply_it: Choose one skill that appears in job adverts for the role you want next, and spend twenty minutes learning it today.

quiz.question: How can you work out which skills to learn next?
options: Only learn what your current job needs today
Wait for your employer to tell you
Look at job adverts and people one or two steps ahead of you
quiz.explanation: The roles you are aiming for show which skills are actually in demand for your path.

cards.title: Find mentors, and in time a sponsor
cards.body:
A mentor is someone more experienced who helps you see your strengths, avoid common traps and spot chances you might miss. You don't need a formal programme. Many great mentors are simply people you admire who agree to a coffee or a call now and then.

Ask for something small and specific: "Could I ask you three questions about how you moved into management?" Come prepared, follow their advice, and later tell them what happened. People enjoy helping someone who acts on their help.

As you grow, look for a sponsor too. A mentor talks to you; a sponsor speaks up for you in rooms where opportunities are decided. Sponsors usually appear when they have seen your good work up close.
cards.apply_it: Name one person whose career you admire. Send them a short, polite message asking for fifteen minutes and one specific question.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a mentor and a sponsor?
options: A mentor pays you, a sponsor doesn't
A mentor advises you; a sponsor speaks up for you where decisions are made
A sponsor is always your direct manager
quiz.explanation: Mentors guide you; sponsors use their influence to put your name forward for opportunities.

cards.title: Build real relationships, not just a contact list
cards.body:
Many opportunities come through people: someone mentions a role, recommends you, or warns you about a bad move. So invest in relationships across your workplace and your field, not just with your boss.

Networking does not have to feel fake. Be curious about what others do, help when you can, share useful information and keep in touch even when you don't need anything. Go to the occasional event or join an online professional group, and have a short, friendly way to say what you do.

Over time, these relationships become your support system. Colleagues who know and trust you are often the ones who say "You should talk to this person" at exactly the right moment.
cards.apply_it: Send a friendly message to one former colleague or classmate today, just to catch up or share something useful.

quiz.question: What makes networking feel genuine rather than fake?
options: Being curious, helping others and keeping in touch
Only contacting people when you need a job
Collecting as many contacts as possible
quiz.explanation: Real relationships are built on interest, generosity and staying in touch over time.

cards.title: Make your work visible without bragging
cards.body:
Good work that nobody sees rarely gets rewarded. Many people assume their results will speak for themselves, but busy managers often miss them. Making your work visible is part of the job.

Keep a simple record of your achievements: what you did, the result, and any numbers, like time saved or customers helped. Share progress in short updates to your manager, especially wins for the team. Offer to present your work at a team meeting.

The key is to focus on results and give credit to others where it is due. "We cut waiting times by a third; I led the new booking system and Amina built the rota" sounds confident and fair, not boastful.
cards.apply_it: Start an achievements note on your phone today and add three things you have done well this month, with results if you can.

quiz.question: Why should you keep a record of your achievements?
options: Because managers often miss good work, and it helps in reviews and promotion talks
quiz.explanation: A clear record helps you share your results and builds your case for reviews, raises and new roles.

cards.title: Ask for feedback before you need it
cards.body:
Most people only hear how they are doing at a yearly review, when it is too late to change much. Instead, ask for feedback regularly, especially after a project or presentation.

Make it easy to answer honestly by being specific: "What is one thing I could do better in client meetings?" works far better than "Any feedback?" Listen without arguing, thank the person, and take a day to think before reacting.

You won't agree with everything, and that is fine. Look for patterns: if two or three people say the same thing, it is worth working on. Then show you acted on it. People keep giving honest feedback to those who clearly use it.
cards.apply_it: Ask one person today: "What is one thing I could do better in [a specific task]?" Then just listen and say thank you.

quiz.question: Which way of asking for feedback usually gets the most useful answer?
options: "What is one thing I could do better in client meetings?"
quiz.explanation: Specific questions make it easier for people to give honest, useful feedback.

cards.title: Say yes to stretch assignments
cards.body:
You grow fastest in work that is a little beyond your current ability. A stretch assignment might be leading a small project, training a new joiner, handling a difficult client or covering for your manager while they are away.

If none come your way, ask. Tell your manager which skills you want to build and offer to take on something that would help. It shows initiative and lets them see you in a bigger role before giving you one officially.

Stretch work will feel uncomfortable, and you may stumble the first time. That is the point. Ask for support early, learn from what goes wrong, and remember that falling short on a stretch task is not the same as failing.
cards.apply_it: Think of one task just beyond your current role that you would like to try. Write a short sentence asking your manager for it.

quiz.question: Why are stretch assignments valuable?
options: They let you build new skills and show you can handle more
quiz.explanation: Work slightly beyond your comfort zone builds skills and lets others see your potential.

cards.title: Set career goals and review them every few months
cards.body:
Without a direction, it is easy to drift for years. You don't need a perfect plan, but you do need a rough idea of where you want to go and the next step towards it.

Think about the role you would like in about five years. Then work backwards: what would you need to have done in three years, and in one year? Note the skills, experience and people that would help at each stage.

Share your goals with your manager or a mentor so they can help. Then check your progress every three months. Plans will change as you learn what you enjoy, and that is fine. The point is to make choices on purpose rather than by accident.
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence describing the job you would like in five years, and one action you can take in the next month towards it.

quiz.question: How often does this guide suggest reviewing your career goals?
options: Only when you lose your job
quiz.explanation: A regular quarterly check helps you adjust your plan and keep moving on purpose.

cards.title: Ask for a promotion or raise with evidence
cards.body:
Promotions and raises are rarely handed out to people who wait silently. When the time is right, usually after a strong period of results, ask for a meeting specifically to discuss it.

Prepare your case. List achievements since your last raise, especially ones that went beyond your goals, with numbers where possible. Research what similar roles pay. Decide on a fair range, not just one figure, and focus on the value you bring, not your personal bills.

In the meeting, stay calm, explain your reasons, then listen. Don't expect an answer on the spot. If the answer is "not now", ask what you would need to show and by when, or suggest a review in a few months. Afterwards, send a short email summarising what was agreed.
cards.apply_it: Write down three achievements from the last six months that you could use to support a request for more pay or responsibility.

quiz.question: What should a request for a pay rise mainly focus on?
options: The value and results you bring, plus market pay
How long you have been waiting
quiz.explanation: A business case built on results and market data is far more persuasive than personal reasons.

cards.title: Shape your personal brand on purpose
cards.body:
Your personal brand is simply what people say about you when you are not in the room. You already have one, so it is worth shaping it.

Decide on two or three things you want to be known for, such as "solves tricky customer problems" or "great at explaining data". Then act in ways that prove it, again and again. Volunteer for work in that area, share what you learn, and help others with it.

Online, make sure your professional profiles are up to date, honest and consistent. Post or comment occasionally on topics in your field. Remember that employers do look you up, so keep your public social media something you would be comfortable showing a future boss.
cards.apply_it: Write down the two things you would most like colleagues to say about you, and one action this week that would prove each.

quiz.question: What is your personal brand?
options: What people say about you when you are not in the room
quiz.explanation: Your reputation is your brand, and you shape it through consistent actions.

cards.title: Know when it is time to move on
cards.body:
Sometimes the best way to grow is to leave. Signs it may be time include: you have stopped learning, there is no realistic path upward, your values clash with the organisation's, or the job is harming your health.

Before deciding, try to fix what you can. Talk to your manager about new responsibilities, ask about other teams, or request training. If nothing changes after a fair attempt, start looking.

Leave well. Search quietly while you keep doing good work, line up a new role before resigning if you can, give proper notice and thank people. Industries are smaller than they look, and the colleagues you leave behind may become future references, clients or bosses.
cards.apply_it: Rate from 1 to 10 how much you are learning in your current role. If it is below 5, list one change you could ask for this month.

quiz.question: What is a wise way to leave a job?
options: Quit suddenly and tell everyone what you think of them
Keep doing good work, give proper notice and leave on good terms
Stop working once you decide to leave
quiz.explanation: Leaving professionally protects your reputation and your future references.
